traveler: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq (Abd Allah ibn Abi Quhafa)
title: The Second of the Two: from the Camel Pens of Mecca to the Chamber Beside the Prophet
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Cloth Merchant of Banu Taym

stops.name: Mecca, the house of Abu Quhafa: a son of Banu Taym
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the biographers give c. 573 and Britannica 573, with no month and no day attested, and no marker survives of the birth site, which is inferred from clan territory alone
stops.campa: In a house of the Banu Taym quarter, a few streets from the Kaaba, a son is born to Abu Quhafa and Umm al-Khayr, and they name him Abd Allah. Mecca will know him better by a nickname earned among the camel pens: Abu Bakr, father of the young camel. He grows into a cloth merchant with a memory for lineages, the man Quraysh consult when they want to know whose grandfather married whose, and the man they trust with a deposit. No document fixes the year and no stone marks the house. The city keeps him without an address.
suggested_refs: The Banu Taym quarter of pre-Islamic Mecca; the pin is approximate, set among the Quraysh households clustered near the Haram

stops.name: Souk Ukaz, the fair on the Ta'if road
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the sources attest attendance at the fair as a customary practice of Meccan traders and not any single year. The dossier placed Ukaz east of Ta'if at 21.5667 / 40.4333; the site lies about 40 km north of the city, between Nakhla and Ta'if, and the pin is corrected
stops.campa: Once a year the tribes lay down their feuds and come to Ukaz, north of Ta'if between Nakhla and the hills, to trade cloth and hides and to hear poets contend for a season's fame. Abu Bakr comes as a merchant and as a merchant's son, and he comes as a genealogist, since a fair is where lineages are recited and disputed and priced. He learns there what every Arab of standing must know: who is descended from whom, and what that is worth. The knowledge will be an instrument of government within forty years.
suggested_refs: Souk Okaz, the annual market and poetry gathering of the Hijaz, revived on its historic ground in the modern era

stops.name: Busra, the caravan road into Syria
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the sources attest the pattern of his trade and not any single journey or year
stops.campa: Long before there is anything to believe, the roads carry him north. Quraysh caravans run cloth and hides and incense up the Hijaz to Busra in the Byzantine province of Syria, and Abu Bakr rides with them, as Muhammad ibn Abd Allah rides with them, two merchants of one city on one road. He learns the price of goods in four markets and the manners of Christian Syria. This corridor is the whole of his known world for thirty years, and it is the corridor his own armies will retrace at the end of his life against the emperor who owns it.
suggested_refs: The Quraysh caravan route from Mecca to Busra, the winter and summer journeys named in Surah Quraysh
sources: general Quraysh caravan-trade tradition, reported in the sira literature

stops.name: Mecca, the house of Muhammad: the assent without argument
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the year is not fixed by the sources, and the order of the earliest converts is disputed between Sunni and Shia tradition while Ibn Kathir declines to rank them at all
stops.campa: Muhammad tells him what came to him on Hira, and Abu Bakr believes without argument. Sunni tradition counts him the first free adult man to enter Islam; Shia tradition gives that place to Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Ibn Kathir sorts the early converts by household rather than rank them. What no source disputes is what follows him in. Uthman ibn Affan, Talha ibn Ubayd Allah, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah come through his advocacy. He is the first man in Mecca whose word is worth something to the new faith, and he spends it.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json, the stop on the first believers of Mecca

segments.name: The Beating, the Buying Back, and the Name

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba: beaten before the sanctuary
stops.date_confidence: traditional, the fourth year of prophethood, c. 613 to 614; the dossier dated the public address to 613 in one lens and c. 615 in another, and the two are harmonised here rather than adjudicated
stops.campa: Muhammad preaches openly in the precinct of the Kaaba, and Abu Bakr stands and speaks after him, the first public address on Islam by anyone but the Prophet. Quraysh youths set on him there, in front of the sanctuary his own clan helps to guard, and beat him until he is carried home senseless. When he comes to, the first thing he asks is whether Muhammad is alive. The atlas gives this same ground to Muhammad's first open preaching and to Abraham raising the foundations of the House.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba pin, 21.4225 / 39.8262, shared byte-identical with muhammad.journey.json, aishah.journey.json and abraham.journey.json among others

stops.name: Mecca, the sand outside the houses: Bilal bought free
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the manumissions are widely attested in the sira and none of them is dated
stops.campa: Umayya ibn Khalaf takes his slave Bilal ibn Rabah out onto the sand beyond the houses, lays him on his back under the noon sun and sets a rock on his chest to make him renounce the one God. Bilal says one word, ahad. Abu Bakr buys him and frees him, and buys and frees others held the same way, and the manumissions eat a merchant's fortune that will never be rebuilt. Muhammad's own journey records this hour from the other side. The tortured slave becomes the voice that will call Medina to prayer.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json; the sources place the torture in open ground outside Mecca, not in a marketplace

stops.name: Bark al-Ghimad, the halt on the Yemen road
stops.date_confidence: traditional, c. 615; the dossier attached Ibn al-Dughunna to the Quraysh boycott of Banu Hashim of 616 to 619, and Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 and 2297 attach him instead to the attempted emigration to Abyssinia, two separate events about two years apart. Bark al-Ghimad is unlocated in any reachable source and the pin only approximates the Yemen road
stops.campa: His fortune worn down by the manumissions, Abu Bakr sets out south for Abyssinia along the Yemen road and gets as far as a halt the sources call Bark al-Ghimad, reckoned five nights out of Mecca. There Ibn al-Dughunna, chief of the Qara, meets him, refuses to let a man of his kind leave Arabia, and takes him back under personal protection. The protection lasts exactly as long as he prays quietly enough for his neighbours not to hear. A year later Quraysh shut the Banu Hashim into their ravine, and he endures that too.
suggested_refs: Sahih al-Bukhari 3905, the hadith of Ibn al-Dughunna's protection; the boycott of the Banu Hashim in the ravine of Abu Talib, 616 to 619

stops.name: Mecca, the house of Abu Bakr: Aishah betrothed
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: In the house of Abu Bakr in the Banu Taym quarter, the betrothal of his daughter Aishah to Muhammad is settled. Aishah's own journey opens in these rooms: a child of the house, born some years into Islam, and the sign Muhammad reports is a form wrapped in silk that an angel showed him. Two families already bound by belief and by the caravan roads become one household in law. Abu Bakr is father-in-law to the Prophet from this year and will be his successor twelve years later, and the two facts will never be argued apart.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from aishah.journey.json, the betrothal in the house of Abu Bakr

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Noble Rock: the name as-Siddiq
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the derivation of the epithet from this answer is tradition, and muhammad.journey.json narrates the ascent without carrying the naming episode
stops.campa: Muhammad tells Mecca he has been carried in a night to the farthest mosque and up through the heavens, and Quraysh bring it to Abu Bakr as a scandal they expect him to disown. He answers that if Muhammad said it then it is true, and that he believes him about far stranger things than this, meaning revelation itself. From that answer the tradition dates his name: as-Siddiq, the one who confirms the truth. The rock stands twelve hundred kilometres north, on ground the atlas gives to Abraham and to Jesus. He is named for a place he never enters.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json, the Isra and Mi'raj at the Temple Mount; jesus.journey.json and abraham.journey.json stand on the same coordinates

stops.name: Mecca, the night the assassins ring the house
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the date is the one carried by muhammad.journey.json and is itself a tradition
stops.campa: Quraysh agree that one man from each clan will strike together, so that no single clan can be held to account for the blood. On the night they come, Muhammad leaves Ali in his bed and walks to the house of Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr has kept two riding camels fed and ready for months against exactly this hour, and weeps when he is told that he is to be the companion. They go out through the back of the house and turn south, away from Medina, because Medina is north and every tracker in Mecca knows it.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json, the Hijra plot

stops.name: Cave of Thawr, three nights in the rock
stops.date_confidence: attested in the hadith corpus and in Quran 9:40 as to the fact; the dates are traditional. The dossier's coordinate for the cave, 21.3775 / 39.8508, differs from the canonical atlas pin by about 5 km, and the canonical pin is kept so that the two journeys sit on one point
stops.campa: They climb Jabal Thawr in the dark and lie up three nights in a cleft near the summit while Quraysh trackers work the slope below, near enough that Abu Bakr can see their feet from inside. His daughter Asma carries food up after dark and ties the sack with half her torn waist-belt, which earns her the name Dhat al-Nitaqayn. His son Abd Allah sleeps in Mecca and brings the night's talk at dawn. Tradition sets a spider's web and a dove's nest across the mouth. The Quran will call him the second of the two.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json and aishah.journey.json; Quran 9:40, 'the second of two, when they were in the cave'

stops.name: Quba, the town comes out to the road
stops.date_confidence: traditional as to the day; September or October 622 is as close as the sources come
stops.campa: They come down the coast road past Qudayd, where a Bedouin woman named Umm Ma'bad gives them milk from a barren goat and knows afterwards who has passed, and they reach Quba on the edge of Yathrib. The town comes out to meet them. The Ansar have watched the road for days, and the tradition says they take Abu Bakr for the Prophet at first because he looks the older of the two, until he stands and shades Muhammad with his cloak and the crowd sorts them out. The first mosque of Islam is laid out here.
suggested_refs: Masjid Quba, the first mosque, raised before the entry into Yathrib; the tent of Umm Ma'bad in the Qudayd valley on the coastal route

stops.name: Al-Sunh, the house among the Banu al-Harith
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the settlement and the trade; the sources give no date for the move and the pin follows the traditional siting of the Sunh suburb
stops.campa: Abu Bakr settles among the Banu al-Harith in the suburb of al-Sunh and goes back to selling cloth rather than live on the community's support. The detail is preserved because it is unusual: the Muhajirun arrive stripped, and most take what the Ansar give. He goes down with the oasis fever in the first months, as the Meccans do, and recovers. From this house he will ride in on the morning Muhammad dies. In this house, twelve years later, the fever will take him for good.
suggested_refs: The Sunh suburb of Medina, unlocated in any modern survey; the pin approximates the quarter of the Banu al-Harith

stops.name: Medina, the mosque: the room against the east wall
stops.date_confidence: traditional, 623 or 624; the sources date the consummation of the marriage only to the first years after the Hijra
stops.campa: Aishah comes up from Mecca with the household and her marriage is consummated in a room built against the eastern wall of the mosque. From this year the household of Abu Bakr lives inside the mosque compound, and her journey and his run through the same doorway. For the next nine years he is never more than a courtyard away from the man he walked out of Mecca beside, and the community learns to read the distance between the two of them as a fact about rank.
stops.quote: If I were to take a Khalil, I would have taken Abu Bakr, but he is my brother and my companion (in Islam).
stops.quote_source: Muhammad on Abu Bakr, narrated by Ibn Abbas; Sahih al-Bukhari 3656, English translation consulted via a sounah.com mirror. The saying is undated in the sources; it is placed here for the Medina years rather than for a particular day.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from aishah.journey.json and muhammad.journey.json, the mosque of Medina and the rooms along its eastern wall

stops.name: Badr, the wells and the shelter on the ridge
stops.date_confidence: attested, 17 Ramadan 2 AH, 13 March 624; the sources divide over whether Abu Bakr stood guard at the Prophet's shelter with a drawn sword or fought in the line, and the divergence is carried rather than settled
stops.campa: Three hundred and some men meet a Quraysh army three times their number at the wells of Badr and break it. Abu Bakr is at the shelter built for the Prophet on the ridge with a drawn sword, and the accounts divide over what that means: some make him a guard at the door of it, others put him in the fighting line. His son Abd al-Rahman is in the ranks opposite, still a Meccan. The Quraysh dead include men he has bought and sold with for thirty years, and he knows every one of their fathers by name.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Badr; the pin sits on the modern town, some kilometres from the traditional site of the wells

stops.name: Uhud, the line breaks and closes
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, Shawwal 3 AH, March 625
stops.campa: The archers leave the hill, Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry comes round behind them, and the Muslim line breaks with a cry going up that Muhammad is dead. Abu Bakr is one of the handful who cut back through to him, find him alive with his face laid open, and get him up the slope out of reach. He takes wounds of his own in the press. Seventy Muslims are left on the field, Hamza among them, speared by a slave named Wahshi ibn Harb. Khalid, who wins this day for Mecca, will be Abu Bakr's own general in eight years.
suggested_refs: The slope of Mount Uhud and the graves of the martyrs; the javelin of Wahshi ibn Harb, thrown twice in this journey

stops.name: Medina, the Trench: a sector held for a month
stops.date_confidence: traditional, Shawwal 5 AH, 627; the sources give the month and not the day
stops.campa: Ten thousand men come up from Mecca and the tribes to finish Medina, and the city digs. On Salman al-Farisi's advice a trench is cut across the open northern approach, and Abu Bakr digs with the rest and then holds a sector of the line through a month of cold and skirmishing. The confederates never cross it. Wind, hunger and their own quarrels break the siege instead. A mosque is built afterwards on the ground he held, which is how Medina remembers who stood where in a war nobody writes down.
suggested_refs: The Masjid Abu Bakr among the Seven Mosques on the trench line, built on the sector he is said to have held

stops.name: Al-Hudaybiyya, the treaty that looks like a defeat
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month and year, Dhu al-Qa'dah 6 AH, March 628; the dossier's coordinates put al-Hudaybiyya south-southeast of Mecca, and the site is identified with modern Ash Shumaysi on the Jeddah road to the northwest, about 35 km from the value given and in the opposite direction
stops.campa: The pilgrims ride for Mecca unarmed and Quraysh stop them at the wells of al-Hudaybiyya, on the Jeddah road northwest of the city. The treaty Muhammad signs reads to the army like a surrender: ten years of truce, no pilgrimage this year, converts fleeing Mecca to be handed back. Umar takes his objection to the Prophet and then to Abu Bakr, who tells him to hold to the man's stirrup and not let go. Abu Bakr does not need the terms explained to him twice, and the Quran will call the day a clear victory.
suggested_refs: Al-Hudaybiyya, identified with Ash Shumaysi on the Jeddah road; the truce of Dhu al-Qa'dah 6 AH

stops.name: Khaybar, the forts and a contested banner
stops.date_confidence: attested as to season, Muharram 7 AH, 628; the banner story is a partisan topos and its Bukhari source names Ali without naming any failed assault by Abu Bakr, which comes from Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi
stops.campa: The oasis of Khaybar holds out fort by fort behind basalt walls, and the siege runs for weeks. One tradition, carried hardest by the partisans of Ali, sends Abu Bakr against the fortress of al-Qamus with the banner and has him come back without taking it, and Umar after him the next day, before the banner passes to Ali and the gate falls. The story is old and it is told for a purpose, attached to the hadith of the banner given to a man who loves God. What is not in dispute is that Abu Bakr is at Khaybar and that Khaybar falls.
suggested_refs: The basalt forts of the Khaybar oasis and the partisan literature attached to al-Qamus
sources: Ibn Ishaq, in Ibn Hisham's recension
al-Bukhari, Sahih, the hadith of the banner

stops.name: Dhat al-Salasil, a ranker on the northern frontier
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, Jumada al-Ula 8 AH, September 629; the dossier made Abu Ubayda supreme commander, and the sources give supreme command of the whole force to Amr ibn al-As, with Abu Ubayda leading only the 200-man reinforcement column and ceding command on arrival. The camp is not fixed in the sources and the pin approximates the frontier zone
stops.campa: Amr ibn al-As is sent north against the tribes on the Syrian frontier and asks for more men. Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah brings up two hundred, Abu Bakr and Umar among them, and on arrival hands command to Amr rather than dispute it. That handover is the whole of Dhat al-Salasil; no engagement is fought. Abu Bakr, who brought Abu Ubayda into Islam and will one day send him against an emperor, serves this campaign as a ranker under a man half his age.
suggested_refs: The raid of Dhat al-Salasil, Jumada al-Ula 8 AH; the exact camp location is not fixed in the sources

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba: the city taken without a battle
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, 20 Ramadan 8 AH, January 630
stops.campa: Ten thousand come down on Mecca and the city opens without a battle. Abu Bakr rides in at fifty-seven, past the pens where he earned his nickname, past the ground where he was beaten senseless for speaking, past the sand where he bought Bilal, who now climbs onto the roof of the Kaaba to give the call. The idols around the House are pulled down and broken. He leads his blind father Abu Quhafa out to give allegiance, and Muhammad tells him he should have left the old man at home and come to him instead.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba pin, shared byte-identical with muhammad.journey.json, aishah.journey.json, abraham.journey.json, ibn_battuta.journey.json and abdelkader.journey.json among others

stops.name: Hunayn, the ambush in the defile
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, Shawwal 8 AH, February 630; the dossier's latitude of 21.35 sits about 9 km south of the valley and is corrected to 21.433
stops.campa: Hawazin archers hold the narrow mouth of the valley and empty it into the column as it comes through. The new Meccan converts run. About nine men hold the ground around Muhammad while the line reforms behind them, and Abu Bakr is one of the nine. It is the last battle of his life in which he is a man in a fight rather than a man who signs orders. Two years on, tribes broken here will be among the first to renounce Medina, and he will send Khalid after them.
suggested_refs: The valley of Hunayn between Mecca and Ta'if, and the rout of the opening hour

stops.name: Ta'if, the dream read and the siege lifted
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month and year, Shawwal 8 AH; the dossier said Abu Bakr led the siege, and the sources have Muhammad leading it in person with Abu Bakr advising. The duration is reported as fifteen to about twenty days, not uniformly two weeks
stops.campa: The survivors of Hawazin shut themselves into Ta'if behind walls the Muslims have no engines to break, and the siege runs somewhere between fifteen and twenty days. Muhammad leads it himself. Abu Bakr's part is a reading: asked what a dream means, he says it means Thaqif cannot be taken this year, and counsels lifting the siege. The counsel is taken and the army marches away without a breach. Ta'if is never stormed. The Banu Thaqif come in afterwards of their own accord.
stops.quote: O Messenger of God, I don't think that you will attain what you desire from them today.
stops.quote_source: The History of al-Tabari, vol. 9 (SUNY Press translation), p. 24, consulted via an archive.org full-text scan. Tabari's framing is only that Abu Bakr addresses Muhammad regarding a group of people during the Prophet's lifetime; the attachment to Ta'if is this atlas's inference from sense and period and is not stated in the source.
suggested_refs: The walls of Ta'if and the siege of Shawwal 8 AH; Wikipedia, 'Siege of Ta'if'

stops.name: Mina, amir al-hajj and a proclamation read by another
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year, Dhu al-Hijja 9 AH; the dossier had the proclamation made on Abu Bakr's order, and both Sunni and Shia retellings turn on the opposite point, that the verses came down after the caravan left and had to be read by the Prophet or by his own house
stops.campa: Muhammad appoints him amir al-hajj, and Abu Bakr assumes ihram at Dhu al-Hulayfa and leads some three hundred pilgrims down to Mecca, the first hajj administered by Muslims since the conquest. At Mina, Ali overtakes the caravan carrying the opening verses of Surah Bara'a and reads them to the assembled tribes: after this year no idolater performs the pilgrimage and no one circles the House naked. Abu Bakr commands the rite. Ali reads the text. Both facts will be cited by people arguing about succession.
suggested_refs: Dhu al-Hulayfa, the pilgrim station now called Abyar Ali; the valley of Mina and the proclamation of Surah Bara'a in 9 AH

stops.name: Medina, the mosque: leading the prayer in the Prophet's illness
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact and the month, Safar to Rabi al-Awwal 11 AH; that the instruction was a signal about succession is a later Sunni reading and is not in the hadith itself
stops.campa: The fever takes hold in Aishah's room and Muhammad can no longer walk out to the prayer. He orders Abu Bakr to lead it. Aishah asks twice for somebody else, saying her father is a soft-hearted man who will never get through the recitation for weeping, and is told twice to let Abu Bakr lead. He leads through the last days of the illness, with the sick man sometimes carried out to pray behind him. Whether this is an instruction about prayer or an instruction about succession is the question the next fourteen centuries divide over.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json and aishah.journey.json, the mosque and the rooms along its eastern wall

stops.name: Medina, the Sacred Chamber: the death of Muhammad
stops.date_confidence: attested, 12 Rabi al-Awwal 11 AH, 8 June 632
stops.campa: On a Monday in June, in the chamber against the east wall of the mosque, Muhammad dies leaning on Aishah. Umar stands in the courtyard with his sword and says he will cut the legs off any man who claims the Prophet is dead. Abu Bakr rides in from al-Sunh, goes past him into the room, uncovers the face, kisses it and covers it again, then comes out and speaks, and recites the verse about a messenger before whom messengers have passed away. Aishah, in her own journey, watches from these rooms as the faith she was born inside changes hands.
stops.quote: Whoever amongst you worshipped Muhammad, then Muhammad is dead, but whoever worshipped Allah, Allah is alive and will never die.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr in the mosque at Medina immediately after Muhammad's death, followed by his recitation of Qur'an 3:144; Sahih al-Bukhari 1241, Kitab al-Jana'iz, Muhsin Khan translation consulted via Daily Hadith Online and an IIUM mirror.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from muhammad.journey.json and aishah.journey.json, al-Hujra al-Sharifa

stops.name: Saqifa Bani Sa'ida, the roofed courtyard
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the day; the exact plot of the Saqifa is not preserved and the pin approximates the traditional site near the mosque
stops.campa: While the body lies unwashed, the Ansar gather under the roofed courtyard of the Banu Sa'ida to choose a leader from among themselves. Abu Bakr, Umar and Abu Ubayda walk in uninvited. Abu Bakr argues that the Arabs will follow no house but Quraysh, and offers the other two men in his own place; Umar takes his hand and swears to him instead, and the room follows. Shia historiography reads the same hour as a seizure carried out over a corpse. The two accounts have never been reconciled and are not reconciled here.
suggested_refs: The Saqifa of the Banu Sa'ida; a marker near the mosque approximates the traditional site

stops.name: Medina, the mosque: the inaugural address
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the address and its occasion; the day after the Saqifa is the traditional placing. Ali and a group with him withhold allegiance for a period given as about six months in largely Shia-derived accounts and as much shorter in Sunni ones
stops.campa: The community at large gives the oath in the mosque, and Abu Bakr becomes the first of the four whom Sunni Islam will call the Rightly Guided. He stands up and tells them what the office is: not the best of them, correctable, obeyed only for as long as he obeys. Ali and a group with him hold back before acknowledging him, for six months in some accounts and for days in others. In Aishah's journey the same morning reads from inside, the office passing out of her husband's hands and into her father's.
stops.quote: To proceed: O people, I have been put in authority over you, but I am not the best of you. If I do the right thing, then help me. If I do wrong, then correct me. Truthfulness is a sacred trust, and lying is a betrayal. The weak among you are strong in my sight so I will relieve their suffering as is their right, if Allah wills. The strong among you are weak in my sight so I will take what is due from them, if Allah wills. No people abandon jihad in the way of Allah but that Allah strikes them with disgrace. Obscenity never spreads among people but that Allah afflicts them with trials. Obey me as long as I obey Allah and His Messenger, but if I disobey Allah and His Messenger, then you are not obligated to obey me. Now, stand for your prayer, and may Allah have mercy upon you.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr's inaugural address after his selection at Saqifat Bani Sa'ida, Medina, 632; Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah 2/661, English rendering consulted via Daily Hadith Online, compiler Abu Amina Elias.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from aishah.journey.json and muhammad.journey.json, the mosque of Medina

stops.name: Medina, the claim to Fadak refused
stops.date_confidence: traditional as to month; the sources date the dispute only to the months after Muhammad's death, and the estrangement is said to have run until Fatima's death six months later
stops.campa: Fatima comes to him for her father's estate: the Fadak oasis, the Khaybar share, the properties in Medina. Abu Bakr refuses her, citing a saying of the Prophet that prophets leave nothing to be inherited, and telling her he will not depart from anything the Messenger did. The hadith says she did not speak to him again before her death six months later. Twelver Shia Islam has never accepted the refusal. Aishah, who narrates the report, is the daughter of one party and the widow of the man whose estate is in dispute.
stops.quote: Our property cannot be inherited, and whatever we leave is to be spent in charity.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr quoting Muhammad to Fatima and al-Abbas; Sahih al-Bukhari 6725, narrated by Aisha, English translation consulted via a sounah.com mirror. His second answer in the same hadith: 'By Allah, I will not leave the procedure I saw Allah's Messenger following during his lifetime concerning this property.'
suggested_refs: The Fadak oasis in the Hejaz, and the long Sunni and Shia literature on its ownership

stops.name: Dhu al-Qassa, the muster on the Najd road
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the month, July to August 632; ancient Dhu al-Qassa is placed about 36 km east of Medina and has not been precisely relocated on modern maps, so the pin is approximate
stops.campa: The tribes that gave zakat to Muhammad will not give it to Abu Bakr, and much of Arabia offers Medina the prayer without the payment. He refuses the terms and marches out himself, with what troops Medina still has, to the staging camp a day's ride east of the city on the Najd road. The companions talk him out of taking the field in person and he hands the columns to Khalid ibn al-Walid. It is the last time he leaves Medina. Everything after this happens because a letter goes out from a room.
suggested_refs: The muster ground of Dhu al-Qassa, staging point of the Ridda columns

stops.name: Buzakha, the coalition of Tulayha broken
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, September 632; the traditional siting near Ha'il is approximate
stops.campa: Khalid takes the Asad and the Ghatafan and their allies at Buzakha in north-central Najd, where Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid has been prophesying and drawing the tribes of the centre together. The coalition breaks and Tulayha rides for Syria; years later he comes back a Muslim and fights for this caliphate in Iraq. Uyayna ibn Hisn is sent to Medina in chains and pardoned there. Abu Bakr issues the columns and the pardons from the same room, and never sees the ground on which either is decided.
stops.quote: Strive for death, then you will be given life.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Abu Bakr addressing Khalid ibn al-Walid, cited to Ibn Abd Rabbih, al-'Iqd al-Farid 1/92 through a Wikiquote compilation. [R]: the primary translated text was not reached, and the saying circulates chiefly in modern military-history retellings of the Ridda wars.
suggested_refs: The wells of Buzakha in Najd; the rival-prophet movements of Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid and of Sajah bint al-Harith

stops.name: Medina, the sword that is not sheathed
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the exchange; the affair of Malik ibn Nuwayra is dated 632 to 633 and falls between Buzakha and Yamama in the campaign sequence, without a fixed day
stops.campa: Khalid kills Malik ibn Nuwayra of the Yarbu at al-Butah and marries his widow in the same week. Umar comes to Abu Bakr and says the man is a murderer and must be dismissed, and says it more than once. Abu Bakr pays the blood money out of the treasury, reprimands Khalid, and keeps him in command, because he has one general who wins and a peninsula in revolt. The two men who make this judgment will be caliph one after the other, and the second of them will dismiss Khalid in his first year.
stops.quote: O Umar, I will not sheathe a sword that God has drawn against the unbelievers.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr to Umar after the killing of Malik ibn Nuwayra; The History of al-Tabari, vol. 10 (The Conquest of Arabia, trans. Fred Donner, SUNY), p. 102, isnad al-Sari from Shu'ayb from Sayf from Hisham b. Urwah from his father, verified against the archive.org full text. Umar's words in the same passage: 'In his sword there really is forbidden behavior.' The popular form 'the sword that God has drawn against the infidels' is a loose retelling.
suggested_refs: The affair of Malik ibn Nuwayra at al-Butah, and Umar's later dismissal of Khalid on his own accession
sources: The History of al-Tabari, vol. 10, trans. Fred Donner (SUNY)

stops.name: Aqraba in Yamama, the Garden of Death
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the week, third week of December 632; the dossier gave the killing of Musaylima to Khalid, who commanded the field but did not strike him
stops.campa: Musaylima of the Banu Hanifa holds the richest farmland in Arabia with a revelation of his own and an army to match it. Khalid meets him on the plain of Aqraba and the fighting is the worst the Muslims have known. The Hanifa fall back into a walled garden, a man is thrown over the wall to open the gate from inside, and the place is remembered afterwards as the Garden of Death. Wahshi ibn Harb kills Musaylima with the javelin he threw at Hamza on the slope of Uhud, and Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan takes the head.
suggested_refs: The plain of Aqraba in al-Yamama and the walled garden called Hadiqat al-Mawt

stops.name: Medina, the Book gathered off palm ribs and stones
stops.date_confidence: attested as to sequence, immediately after al-Yamama, which was fought in the third week of December 632; the dossier dated the compilation order a year late, to 633, and the count of huffaz killed is given as roughly 360
stops.campa: Umar comes to Abu Bakr with the count of memorisers killed at Yamama, about three hundred and sixty of them, and says the Book will die with the next battle. Abu Bakr answers that he will not do what the Messenger did not do, and is argued round. He puts it to Zayd ibn Thabit, who says that moving a mountain would be lighter work, and is argued round in his turn. Zayd gathers the text off palm ribs, thin white stones, scraps of leather and the memory of living reciters.
stops.quote: You are a wise young man and we do not have any suspicion about you, and you used to write the Divine Inspiration for Allah's Messenger. So you should search for the fragmentary scripts of the Qur'an and collect it in one book.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr commissioning Zayd ibn Thabit after the losses at al-Yamama; Sahih al-Bukhari 4986, Kitab Fada'il al-Qur'an, narrated by Zayd ibn Thabit, English translation consulted via a sounah.com mirror.
suggested_refs: The first Mus'haf, gathered under Abu Bakr, passed to Umar and then to Hafsa bint Umar; no leaf of it is known to survive

stops.name: Medina, the mosque: a war run from one room
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the campaign sequence, Zafar in January 633 and Nujair in February 633, with the reunification of Arabia dated to March 633
stops.campa: Muhajir ibn Abi Umayya and Ziyad ibn Labid break al-Ash'ath at Zafar, the capital of Hadhramaut, and the fortress of Nujair falls after it, and with that the south is finished and Arabia answers to Medina again. Abu Bakr is at the mosque. He has not been on a battlefield since the muster at Dhu al-Qassa, and no source places him at Buzakha or Yamama or Zafar, or in Bahrayn or Oman or Yemen. The whole geography of the Ridda wars belongs to the men he sent. The war is his.
suggested_refs: The Ridda war geography of Buzakha, Yamama, Zafar, Nujair, Bahrayn, Oman and Yemen, none of which Abu Bakr visits in person

stops.name: Hira, the Lakhmid capital takes terms
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year and the order sending Khalid into Iraq; the dossier attests the campaign and not the individual towns or their dates, and the month here is inferred from the campaign sequence
stops.campa: With the peninsula quiet, Abu Bakr turns Khalid north out of Yamama into Sasanian Iraq, leaving al-Muthanna ibn Haritha to work the frontier with the troops that remain. Khalid takes the desert edge of the Euphrates town by town and comes to Hira, the Lakhmid capital of the Arab Christians, which pays tribute rather than be stormed. It is the first time a Muslim army takes money from a city that was answering to an emperor a month earlier, and the first sign that this is not a raid.
suggested_refs: Al-Hira on the desert edge of the Euphrates, seat of the Lakhmid kings

stops.name: Medina, the road out: ten things told to an army
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; the sources give Rajab 12 AH, September 633, or early 13 AH, spring 634, and the dossier's figure of 24,000 men appears in no source reached and is dropped. The departure point outside Medina is not fixed and the pin uses the mosque
stops.campa: He sends three or four armies into southern Syria and Palestine under Amr ibn al-As, Shurahbil ibn Hasana, Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan and Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, and walks out of Medina beside Yazid's horse to see them off. Yazid offers to dismount and is refused. He gives him ten instructions on the conduct of the campaign instead: what may not be killed, what may not be cut down, what may not be burned, what may not be taken. Thirty years earlier he rode this road himself with a load of cloth.
stops.quote: I advise you ten things: Do not kill women or children or an aged, infirm person. Do not cut down fruit-bearing trees. Do not destroy an inhabited place. Do not slaughter sheep or camels except for food. Do not burn bees and do not scatter them. Do not steal from the booty, and do not be cowardly.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr's instructions to Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan as his army departed for Syria; Muwatta of Imam Malik, Book 21 (Jihad), hadith 21.3.10, English translation consulted via a qurango.com mirror. In the same hadith he refuses to mount: 'I will not ride and you will not get down. I intend these steps of mine to be in the way of Allah.'
suggested_refs: The ten instructions of Abu Bakr, transmitted in the Muwatta of Imam Malik as the earliest Muslim law of war

stops.name: Ajnadayn, the first pitched battle in Syria
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month, July or August 634; the Yarmuk, often credited to Abu Bakr's concentration order, was fought in August 636 under Umar and is not his
stops.campa: Byzantium reinforces, and Abu Bakr orders Khalid out of Iraq to march west across the waterless desert and take command in Syria. The columns concentrate and meet a Byzantine field army at Ajnadayn in Palestine, and win the first pitched battle of the conquest. The corridor is the Busra road he rode as a merchant for thirty years, running now the other way with his own armies on it. The news goes down the Hijaz road to Medina and reaches him in bed, in the last month of his life.
suggested_refs: The field of Ajnadayn in Palestine; Khalid's desert march from Iraq to the Syrian front

stops.name: Medina, the testament dictated
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the sequence; he fell ill on 7 Jumada al-Akhirah 13 AH, 8 August 634, and the illness ran about fifteen days. His house at al-Sunh is unlocated and the pin uses the mosque
stops.campa: The fever holds him about fifteen days. He calls the companions in one at a time and asks them about Umar ibn al-Khattab, and hears the objection that Umar is too hard a man; he answers that the office will soften him. Then he has the appointment written down and read out, so that nobody will have to hold a second Saqifa over his body. He gives instructions too: what remains of his salary goes back to the treasury, and he is to be buried in the clothes he is wearing, washed.
stops.quote: Verily, I appoint over you Umar ibn al-Khattab as my successor, so listen to him and obey him... If he acts justly, then that is what I think of him and that is what I know about him. But if he changes for the worse, then for each person is that which he has earned. Goodness is what I wanted, and I do not know anything of the Unseen world.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr's written testament, dictated to Uthman ibn Affan; English rendering from al-Sallabi, The Biography of Abu Bakr as-Siddeeq (Darussalam), p. 726, citing al-Dhahabi, Tarikh al-Islam, pp. 116-117. The commonly printed tail 'and only Allah knows' has no basis in any source reached, and al-Tabari vol. 11 carries the succession narratives but not this wording.
suggested_refs: The deathbed testament naming Umar, and the objections to his temperament recorded by the companions
sources: al-Sallabi, The Biography of Abu Bakr as-Siddeeq (Darussalam), p. 726, citing al-Dhahabi

stops.name: Medina, death of the first caliph
stops.date_confidence: attested, Monday 22 Jumada al-Akhirah 13 AH, 23 August 634; the dossier gave the Hijri day as 23 in one lens and 22 in another, and 22 is the traditional figure. Age at death is given as 60 in the Wikipedia infobox and as 63 in most classical sources, matching Muhammad's lifespan, and the range 60 to 63 is where the sources leave it
stops.campa: He dies in Medina on the twenty-third of August, of the fever, having governed two years and seventy-seven days, which the chronographers also render as two years, two months and fourteen days, the same interval counted in different units. His rule ran from Yemen to the edge of the Euphrates. He is the only one of the four Rightly Guided caliphs to die in his bed; Umar, Uthman and Ali are all murdered in office. A later story has him poisoned a year in advance, and the chain that carries it does not hold.
suggested_refs: The poisoning tradition, involving al-Harith ibn Kalada and Attab ibn Usayd, flagged by later scholars as lacking a sound chain of transmission

stops.name: Medina, the Sacred Chamber: buried at the Prophet's shoulder
stops.date_confidence: attested, 23 to 24 August 634
stops.campa: Umar leads the funeral prayer and they open the floor of Aishah's chamber beside Muhammad's grave. On Umar's instruction Abu Bakr is laid with his head level with the Prophet's shoulders, which is the tradition's way of saying where it ranks him. Forty-eight hours ago he was governing from Yemen to the Euphrates. Umar takes the office the same day and takes with it the frontier armies, the gathered sheets of the Quran, and the caliphate as something a man can hand on, which nobody knew it was two years ago.
suggested_refs: The pin is inherited byte-identical from aishah.journey.json and muhammad.journey.json, the Sacred Chamber under what became the Green Dome

stops.name: Medina, the dome raised, burned, rebuilt, painted green
stops.date_confidence: attested as to years: 678 AH, 1279 to 1280, for the first dome under Qalawun; 1481 for the fire and the Qaitbay rebuilding; 1818 for the present structure under Mahmud II; 1837 for the paint
stops.campa: Six centuries on, the Mamluk sultan al-Mansur Qalawun raises a dome of bare wood over the chamber that holds three graves. Qaitbay rebuilds it in stone and lead after the fire of 1481. Mahmud II builds the present structure in 1818 and it is painted green in 1837, which is where the name comes from. In 1805 the forces of the Al Saud take Medina and strip the chamber of its gold, and leave the dome standing, whether for the difficulty of pulling it down or for a scruple. Emir Abdelkader prays here in 1825, between the two.
suggested_refs: The Green Dome of al-Masjid an-Nabawi; abdelkader.journey.json places the Emir at the Prophet's tomb in 1825, on his own Medina pin

stops.name: Istanbul, a sword in the Chamber of Sacred Relics
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the transfer, chiefly after the Ottoman conquest of Mamluk Cairo in 1517; the attribution of the individual sword rests on the collection's own tradition and no source reached establishes its provenance
stops.campa: A sword said to be Abu Bakr's hangs in the Chamber of Sacred Relics at Topkapi Palace in Istanbul, with swords attributed to Umar, Uthman and Ali and a cloak attributed to Muhammad. The relics come north chiefly after the Ottoman conquest of Mamluk Cairo in 1517, when the sultans take the guardianship of the holy cities and the objects that went with it. The man who gave away his property and sent his last salary back to the treasury is represented in Istanbul by a weapon.
suggested_refs: The Hirka-i Saadet, Chamber of Sacred Relics, Topkapi Palace, Istanbul
sources: TRT World, 'Why did Ottoman sultans safeguard Islam's holy relics'

stops.name: Jannat al-Baqi, the neighbours levelled
stops.date_confidence: attested, 21 April 1926, though some sources give 1925; the dossier conflated the December 1925 surrender of Medina to Ibn Saud with the demolition itself, and the two are separated here
stops.campa: Medina surrenders to Ibn Saud in December 1925. On the twenty-first of April following, the Ikhwan level the domes and headstones of Jannat al-Baqi, the cemetery a few hundred metres from the mosque where much of the Prophet's family and most of his companions lie, and leave the ground bare earth. The Green Dome, a short walk away, is untouched a second time. In 2007 a pamphlet from the Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs argues that it should come down and the three graves be flattened. It still stands.
suggested_refs: Jannat al-Baqi before 1926 in Ottoman-era pilgrim photographs; the 2007 Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs pamphlet on the Green Dome
